papers.title: ToolBottleneckBench: Measuring Tool-Agent Performance under Controlled Pressures and Fixed Harness Budgets
papers.abstract: The success score of a tool agent reflects both its model and the budgets of the harness that runs it. We present ToolBottleneckBench, a benchmark that measures tool-agent performance under controlled pressures and fixed harness budgets. Synthetic enterprise tasks stay fixed while one pressure varies: the registered tool catalog, the visible tool menu, the certified workflow, or the encoding of returned records. An exact grader records the first unmet obligation of each failed episode and the harness limit, if any, that ended it. Across 21 model and harness configurations, the visible menu is the only one of the three pressures that act on the model with a large penalty, and this penalty tracks truncation at the completion cap. Raising the cap sixteenfold removes most of the penalty in the truncation-heavy configurations. Most failures end at a harness limit, and the failure record identifies the assigned pressure no more reliably than a count of tool calls. The repairs that help change which tools reach the model or who issues the calls, and only two repairs, neither improving model behavior, beat every configuration switch. We recommend reporting pressure effects with the harness budgets under which they were measured. We release the benchmark at https://github.com/zichuanxu/tool-bottleneck-bench.

papers.title: Combining LLM and Dynamic Analysis for Universal Testing of Static Application Security Testing Tools
papers.abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools help detect potential software vulnerabilities, but they themselves contain faults undermining reliability and usability. Automated testing can address these issues, yet current techniques suffer from limited program transformation diversity and lack mechanisms to verify generated variants, leading to reduced fault detection and high manual effort. We present LLM4SAST, the first universal framework detecting faults in SAST tools using large language models and dynamic feedback. Our key insight is leveraging LLMs to understand and transform code in diverse programming languages. We design novel metamorphic relations with transformations to guide variant generation, using an LLM to produce multi-language variants that satisfy these relations. To reduce erroneous variants and identify unique faults, we propose two heuristics: dynamic-feedback-driven selection and program-differencing-based clustering. For each metamorphic relation, a report-centric test oracle detects variants that fail tests and identifies underlying faults by differentially analyzing SAST reports of the seed program and its variants. LLM4SAST identified 66 unique faults across six SAST tools, with 32 confirmed or fixed after being reported to developers, demonstrating effectiveness. The proposed heuristics eliminate 47.8% of false positives, and LLM4SAST detects 3.4 times more faults while requiring only 39.8% of the variants compared to existing approaches.

papers.title: Evaluating and Improving Static Application Security Testing Tools for Rust
papers.abstract: Rust has become a popular systems programming language in recent years because of its strong guarantees on memory and concurrency safety. Many types of system software have been re-implemented in Rust. However, Rust programs can still suffer from common memory and concurrency vulnerabilities due to unsafe code and misunderstandings of its complex mechanisms. To mitigate such vulnerabilities, developers often rely on static application security testing (SAST) tools. However, the effectiveness of existing Rust SAST tools on real-world vulnerabilities remains underexplored. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical evaluation of mainstream Rust SAST tools using security vulnerabilities identified in real-world Rust applications. We systematically assess their effectiveness, uncover common weaknesses, and analyze the root causes behind them. Motivated by the study, we propose TRUST, a large language model (LLM)-assisted automated testing framework. TRUST automatically analyzes the official Rust reference to derive and implement semantics-preserving transformations. It leverages these transformations to generate mutant programs for evaluating Rust SAST tools and uncovering potential faults within them. Overall, TRUST has revealed 46 faults across six popular SAST tools, 17 of which have been confirmed. In addition, our study yields ten empirical findings and four practical lessons that provide actionable guidance for developing more effective, robust, and maintainable Rust SAST tools.

papers.title: Independent Data-Integrity Verification for LLM-Driven Functional Coverage Closure in Hardware Design
papers.abstract: LLM agents can write directed tests that close functional coverage, but coverage only shows that a state was reached, not that the data on the way there was correct. This is a long-known point in verification and we do not claim it as new. We describe a small coverage-closure agent that applies it to an LLM loop: coverage is read from the report that the simulation itself exports (cocotb-coverage YAML) and never taken from the model's account, and data integrity is checked by scoreboards that are separate from the model. On three architecturally distinct RTL designs (an asynchronous FIFO, a UART transmitter and an AHB2APB bridge) the agent raised coverage from 91.7%, 88.9% and 67.4% to 100% within its 8-iteration budget in every logged run, using one design-agnostic agent. A reactive scoreboard monitor attached to the FIFO's base testbench also found a clock-domain-crossing bug in the author's own stimulus code. The monitor is not yet attached to the LLM-generated tests, so their data integrity is not independently checked; one manual check on a single FIFO test is reported as preliminary. We list the weaknesses of this evidence: three designs, no baseline, no ablation, and logged runs that come from several agent checkpoints.

papers.title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
papers.abstract: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer systems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. FDE-Gym scores a delivery by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time). An online platform lets humans practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting, where unstated constraints must be discovered, the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). Discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover them without explicit guidance. Yet information discovery alone does not account for the gap: even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtains every key fact from stakeholders, it reaches a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10. These results reveal a substantial gap between solving well-specified tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers.

papers.title: Where the SRAM Goes: Per-Symbol Attribution of Static Memory in FreeRTOS-C and Embassy-Rust IoT Firmware on a 64 KB RISC-V Microcontroller
papers.abstract: Selecting a firmware stack for a memory-constrained microcontroller is usually guided by aggregate binary sizes, which report how much SRAM a build consumes but not where it goes or why. We address that gap with a per-symbol attribution method that decomposes static RAM into architectural categories - scheduler heap, network buffers and pools, task stacks, and linker-reserved regions - by bounding sized ELF symbols to the .data, .bss and .stack section ranges. The method is validated by reconciling every category sum exactly against the size-based totals for all sixteen builds. We apply it to eight cumulative firmware milestones, from a bare task scaffold to a full MQTT-over-Ethernet client, implemented twice, in FreeRTOS-C and in Embassy-Rust, on the CH32V203RBT6, a RISC-V microcontroller with 64 KB SRAM and an on-chip Ethernet MAC and PHY, with functional parity verified on hardware at every milestone. The decomposition shows that both stacks spend a nearly identical share of their RAM on networking (63.8% versus 63.9%), yet the absolute cost differs by 4.4 times: 40,719 bytes for lwIP against 9,316 bytes for smoltcp. FreeRTOS task stacks grow linearly at roughly 1 KB per task while Embassy async state grows with state-machine complexity. We also report that lwIP could not be integrated under an all-static discipline on this platform, requiring a 20 KB arena that smoltcp does not. The measurement harness, the attribution tool, and the sixteen firmware implementations are released as artefacts.

papers.title: Poison Valleys: Diagnosing Path-Dependent Failure in LLM Code Repair
papers.abstract: When code-repair agents fail, final tests reveal that a patch is wrong but not which earlier commitment caused it or which software obligation failed. Poison Valleys traces this path in 1,844 model requests on two synthetic Python cases: PersistQueue adds atomic batch claiming to a disk-backed queue, while Dijkstra adds source-sensitive filtering to shortest-path search. We define plausible but incorrect software mechanisms, place each in a model's hypothesis, implementation plan, or both, and evaluate the generated code with an Oracle and targeted diagnostic coordinates. Moving the misconception from hypothesis to plan increased failure by 32.2% in PersistQueue and 28.9% in Dijkstra after matching the experimental mix. Different misconceptions produced distinct, model-dependent patterns of violated obligations, although several could converge on the same behavior. This creates a measured connection from upstream misconception to code mechanism and failure form. Code, data, and demo: https://poisonvalleys.org.

papers.title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
papers.abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint. Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept. Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size. Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score. Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920

papers.title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents
papers.abstract: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.

papers.title: Enhancing Knowledge Density via Hierarchical Context Pruning for Retrieval-Augmented Repository-Level Code Completion
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has advanced repository-level code completion by retrieving external code snippets, API documentation, or type definitions to expand the model's contextual awareness. However, under the finite token budget of the context window, existing retrieval-augmented methods often saturate the budget with highly similar or even redundant code, which not only wastes tokens but also suppresses critical cross-file dependencies, preventing synergistic interaction between semantically similar reference snippets and cross-file dependency definitions. Therefore, further gains are limited by low knowledge density in the retrieved context rather than by model capacity. We propose SaraCoder, a retrieval-augmented framework that enhances knowledge density via hierarchical context pruning under a fixed context budget. A Hierarchical Feature Optimization module prunes an over-complete candidate pool in four stages. The freed tokens are then allocated to an External-Aware Identifier Disambiguator, which selectively injects only the most necessary cross-file dependency definitions. SaraCoder transforms context construction into a budget-aware optimization problem, balancing reference snippets and cross-file dependencies to build a context that is both knowledge-dense and semantically complete. Experiments on CrossCodeEval and RepoEval-Updated, across multiple backbone code LLMs, show that SaraCoder consistently outperforms strong RAG baselines such as GraphCoder and Repocoder in both code-level and identifier-level metrics, without increasing token usage, and yields synergistic gains when combined with other cross-file methods.

papers.title: RAG4Tickets: AI-Powered Ticket Resolution via Retrieval-Augmented Generation on JIRA and GitHub Data
papers.abstract: Modern software teams frequently encounter delays in resolving recurring or related issues due to fragmented knowledge scattered across JIRA tickets, developer discussions, and GitHub pull requests (PRs). To address this challenge, we propose a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that integrates Sentence-Transformers for semantic embeddings with FAISS-based vector search to deliver context-aware ticket resolution recommendations. The approach embeds historical JIRA tickets, user comments, and linked PR metadata to retrieve semantically similar past cases, which are then synthesized by a Large Language Model (LLM) into grounded and explainable resolution suggestions. The framework contributes a unified pipeline linking JIRA and GitHub data, an embedding and FAISS indexing strategy for heterogeneous software artifacts, and a resolution generation module guided by retrieved evidence. Experimental evaluation using precision, recall, resolution time reduction, and developer acceptance metrics shows that the proposed system significantly improves resolution accuracy, fix quality, and knowledge reuse in modern DevOps environments.

papers.title: Benchmarking Code LLM-as-a-Judge via Constrained Perturbation and Calibration
papers.abstract: Code from LLM-assisted development may contain defects like API hallucinations, motivating the development of code evaluation metrics to assess such code before deployment. As conventional rule-based metrics merely score code based on similarity to reference programs, and execution-based metrics require expensive manual preparation for tests, researchers have developed LLM-as-a-judge metrics for both behavioral and nonbehavioral code evaluation, and curated multiple benchmarks to validate their effectiveness. However, such benchmarks suffer from critical limitations: Some feature coarse-grained binary labels of passing/failing unit tests, unable to distinguish between fundamental and minor flaws; others utilize fine-grained criteria with manually annotated scores as ground-truth, but such criteria are often vaguely defined, introducing subjectivity and unreliability in human scores. Furthermore, they often directly prompt LLMs to generate code for evaluation, which may lead to unbalanced code quality distributions, failing to test the metrics' discriminative capability across varying quality levels. To curate a diverse benchmark with a balanced program quality distribution and streamline manual annotation, we propose AXIOM, a novel perturbation-based framework. It reframes program scores as the refinement effort needed for deployment, with two stages: (1) Quality-constrained semantic perturbation, prompting LLMs to apply sequences of predefined perturbation rules to existing programs, precisely controlling each program's target quality to achieve a balanced distribution. (2) Hybrid quality calibration, selecting semantically distinct programs for benchmark diversity, and performing streamlined manual annotation with multisource context. With AXIOM, we curate AXIOMBENCH, a large-scale multilingual benchmark with 1,962 code evaluation problems in a more balanced score distribution...

papers.title: LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Language to Leverage Structure and Semantics at the LLM Interface
papers.abstract: Textual Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a simple and familiar interface: a string of text is used for both input and output. However, the information conveyed to an LLM often has a richer structure and semantics, which is not conveyed in a string. For example, most prompts contain both instructions ("Summarize this paper into a paragraph") and data (the paper to summarize), but these are usually not distinguished when passed to the model. This can lead to model confusion and security risks, such as prompt injection attacks. This work addresses this shortcoming by introducing an LLM-native mark-up language, LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "Lemon"), that enables the structure and semantic metadata of the text to be communicated in a natural way to an LLM. This information can then be used during model training, model prompting, and inference implementation, leading to improvements in model accuracy, safety, and security. This is analogous to how programming language types can be used for many purposes, such as static checking, code generation, dynamic checking, and IDE highlighting. We discuss the general design requirements of an LLM-native markup language, introduce the LLMON markup language and show how it meets these design requirements, describe how the information contained in a LLMON artifact can benefit model training and inference implementation, and provide some preliminary empirical evidence of its value for both of these use cases. We also discuss broader issues and research opportunities that are enabled with an LLM-native approach.

papers.title: ORACLE-SWE: Quantifying the Contribution of Critical Information Signals on SWE Agents
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Language Model (LM) agents have increasingly focused on repository-level software engineering (SWE) tasks, leading to various agentic workflows, training methods and failure analysis. Interestingly, rather than directly generating or evaluating edit patches, these approaches first examine and improve intermediate information signals collected during agent exploration, including Reproduction Test, Regression Test, Edit Location, Execution Context, and API Usage. Although different studies examine different subsets of these signals, no work has systematically compared their relative effectiveness in improving final task success or measured the remaining space for improvement in each signal. To address this gap, this work quantifies the contributions of both oracle and agent-extracted signals to final task success and measures the gap between current agent-found signals and their oracle counterparts. We hope our findings could suggest future research emphasis in SWE agents. We release our source code and oracle-signal dataset as a reusable methodology to benefit future signal analysis of SWE agents.

papers.title: Don't Regenerate, Debug: A Domain-Specific Agent for Repairing Near-Miss Accelerator Kernels
papers.abstract: Kernel generation for hardware accelerators such as GPUs and NPUs has become a proving ground for large language models (LLMs), and state-of-the-art systems raise correctness through pipelines that couple LLMs with agentic reinforcement learning and evolutionary search. Such pipelines generate, compile, and execute large numbers of candidate kernels, discarding most of them and forgoing the opportunity to distill failures into reusable knowledge. Many discarded candidates are near-miss operators that compile and run but fail numerical validation; each embodies genuine domain knowledge and a nontrivial investment in LLM inference, cross-compilation, and hardware execution. We argue for a paradigm shift: rather than regenerate, debug. Debugging is far more constrained than generating from scratch: the search space is small and feedback is dense. We present a domain-specific debug agent that addresses three core challenges in autonomous repair: mitigating knowledge scarcity through retrieved patterns and diagnostic instrumentation, ensuring integrity through anti-cheat detection and full-coverage evaluation, and controlling cost via convergence guards and bounded iteration. Debugging serves two complementary roles: it extends the capability frontier by recovering operators that repeated regeneration fails to produce, and it lowers cost per deliverable operator. Debug Pass@1 achieves 66.7% versus Regenerate Avg Pass@1's 25.9% and Regenerate Pass@3's 40.7%, while consuming 92.8% fewer tokens per success than three-trial regeneration. Component ablations show that the knowledge base drives recovery, while integrity gates reject 12.5-33.3% of the successes the workflow itself accepted.

papers.title: Spec-Driven Development as Prescribed and as Practiced
papers.abstract: AI coding agents implement software from naturallanguage instructions, but the intent behind that work is lost when stated only in chat sessions. Spec-driven development (SDD) addresses this by having developers and agents write specifications that guide implementation, yet evidence on its use comes largely from tool vendors. We study SDD in practice through a thematic analysis of Reddit discussions, interviews with 21 practitioners, including eight tool makers, and 266 active and popular repositories in SpecMine, a corpus of 470,795 spec files from 73,030 public GitHub repositories that we release. Practitioners agreed that specs should capture intent, but many also included implementation details, used SDD selectively and mainly for new features, and reported more reliable agent behavior alongside greater planning and review costs. Our findings show that implementation detail may help agents while making specs prone to decay, that tool-specific record structures shape what people and agents see, and that participants described spec-code checks mainly when changes are completed rather than over time. We also find that individual benefits may come from clarifying intent before delegation, while team benefits may depend on SDD becoming a shared process. We derive implications for tool builders, practitioners, and researchers.

papers.title: A Model-Centric DevOps Architecture for DEVS-Based Digital Twin Simulation Services
papers.abstract: Digital twin simulation models evolve and are redeployed like software. Engines based on the Discrete Event System Specification (DEVS) have a sound formal basis but offer little support for versioning, automated validation, or continuous delivery in cloud-native environments. This paper proposes a model-centric DevOps architecture that deploys DEVS-based digital twin simulations as managed services. Models are first-class DevOps artefacts written in a declarative language based on YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) with a tuple-level mapping to the multiPDEVS formalism. Repository continuous integration (CI) validates publishing manifests, the engine loader performs syntactic, structural, and static semantic checks before every simulation, and published model artefacts are versioned and immutable, so that an earlier validated version can be selected by pinning its identifier. The platform runs as containerised microservices on Kubernetes with engine adaptations that externalise inputs and results and expose lifecycle control. An initial case study on bus route 22 in Riga exercises the lifecycle on an offline model with roughly 115,000 DEVS atomic components and reports single-container throughput and concurrent job execution on one Kubernetes node. Behavioural validation and multi-node evaluation remain future work.

papers.title: SWE-Nexus: Automated Composition of Software Engineering Tasks from Test Execution
papers.abstract: Historical code changes provide convenient task boundaries, but do not identify which production functions selected tests exercise or support composing validated behaviors beyond a single change. We present SWE-Nexus, a fully automated pipeline that constructs repository-level implementation tasks from test execution. Four construction agents select tests, adapt tracing and evaluation protocols to each repository, and generate behavioral specifications. For each selected test file, tracing records an observed execution footprint of production function bodies. A scope is retained only if all expected scoring points pass in the original repository and masking the traced bodies causes at least one failure or error. Compatible scopes are composed deterministically, with shared functions counted once and every constituent test file revalidated under the complete combined mask. The benchmark contains 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages, including 116 atomic and 484 composite tasks. We evaluate 12 models under three agent scaffolds. The best configuration resolves 37.8% of tasks in one attempt, and scope-weighted scoring measures partial recovery. SWE-Nexus enables task construction from validated behavior beyond individual historical changes.

papers.title: Harnessing MPI mutations for AI error detection
papers.abstract: MPI errors are challenging to identify despite the significant number of expert verification tools. Dynamic tools (i.e., requiring profiling) are computationally expensive and accurate in error detection, whereas static analysis (i.e., operating at source code or compilation) is computationally cheap but less accurate. Interestingly, the recent success of AI and LLMs offers an alternative to increase static analysis accuracy while preserving its low overhead. Yet current methods remain difficult to benchmark, too general, and poorly adapted to the specific challenges of high-performance computing. In this paper, we investigate how AI-powered tools can efficiently and accurately detect errors in real-world MPI applications. We propose a novel MPI Mutated Dataset (MMD), constructed from MPI programs extracted from thousands of open-source GitHub projects. After sorting and filtering these files, we inject errors that realistically emulate developers' mistakes using synthetic code mutations. We leverage the dataset to train different AI models and assess their generalization capabilities against standard verification tools. We train compact multilayer perceptrons (MLP) with AST-T5 embeddings (i.e., transformer only encoder network) to detect diverse MPI errors (from the MPI-BugBench (MBB) classification) including CallOrdering or InvalidParameter, achieving detection accuracies up to 92.0%. In some cases, our method outperforms the expert prompted Qwen-3 Coder LLM and provides competitive results compared to established dynamic verification tools. We further evaluate Claude Sonnet 4.5 across different prompting strategies, showing that engineered prompts improve InvalidParam detection accuracy from 84.8% to 93.6%, surpassing the dynamic tool ITAC (87.0%). The full agentic pipeline achieves 73.9% overall multi-class accuracy and 87.6% bug detection recall on MBB. This paves the way for large-scale verification efforts that can use our dataset as a foundation to thoroughly investigate each MPI error in real world applications.

papers.title: Testing and Verification of Quantum Compilers through Assurance Contracts and Evidence
papers.abstract: Quantum compiler assurance requires a semantic relation that matches the intended use and observations that can expose violations at the delivered interface. This critical integrative survey compares verified transformations, equivalence checking, differential and metamorphic testing, property-based testing, and evidence for assurance across revisions. A source catalogue and focused extraction matrix distinguish formal guarantees, reported empirical findings, analytical deductions, and proposed practice. A recorded coverage update and source-level selection decisions make the review auditable within its declared scope. Four documented failure cases connect conditional applicability, parameter association, termination, and phase conventions to method selection. A worked example involving layout metadata, parameter bindings, and ancillary qubits demonstrates why validating a circuit under a reconstructed interpretation can leave the delivered interface unchecked. An illustrative revision scenario then separates fault detection from change attribution. The resulting guidance specifies applicability, complementary observations, and treatment of inconclusive outcomes. Published bug counts, mutation results, and processing benchmarks support different claims and do not establish a common effectiveness ranking. The proposed regression architecture remains unevaluated as a complete system; its practical value requires controlled comparisons on independently adjudicated compiler-change events.

papers.title: Causal Syntax Circuits in CodeLMs: Budget and Probe Decide What Looks Localised
papers.abstract: Code models write Python when the prompt does not say which language to use. We ask a mechanistic question about that habit: is it produced by a small, findable group of components inside the model? We run one pipeline---mean ablation, activation patching, greedy circuit extraction, a random-control significance test, and activation steering---over 55 model-language settings spanning ten open code models (five base and five instruction-tuned), three target languages (Rust, C#, PHP), two prompt suites, and two component budgets. We report five findings. First, the preference is large, grows with model size, and survives instruction tuning: it is larger on every instruction-tuned checkpoint than on its base version, by 12% on average. Second, its measured size is mostly a property of the probe; replacing our aligned prompts with XLCoST parallel functions takes the same measurement on the same models from about 1.6 to about 0.01. Third, whether the preference looks localised depends on how many components the search may keep: with a budget of 12, 1 of 15 settings yields a circuit that beats size-matched random controls after multiple-comparison correction, and with a budget of 40, 6 of 15 do. Fourth, interventions that a smaller-budget study reports as uniformly failing do sometimes succeed: patching makes a Python prompt prefer target syntax in 2 of 45 settings, and steering changes the most likely next token in 9 of 45. Fifth, every circuit whose effect is significant but points away from the target language comes from a setting where circuit extraction failed, which makes such results a diagnostic rather than a phenomenon. The practical lesson is that a claim about whether a behaviour is localised can turn on analysis choices that papers rarely report. We release the full grid so those choices can be varied.

papers.title: Stateful Testing for Deep Learning Compilers
papers.abstract: Modern deep learning compilers compile models lazily and cache artifacts across invocations. Retained compiler state can make a later invocation incorrect even when it is correct in isolation. An analysis of 26 publicly reported issues in PyTorch, JAX, and TensorFlow shows that detecting such bugs requires sequences that first establish compiler state and then expose a failure. We present Rondo, a stateful testing method that represents each test case as a model paired with an invocation sequence. Rondo mutates invocation sequences and uses a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler guided by compilation behavior to favor rarely observed behaviors. Its three-way differential oracle compares execution without compilation, compiled execution with compiler state reset, and compiled execution with state retained. It confirms stateful bugs by replaying the same invocation with state retained and reset while preserving inputs and program state, then shortens sequences while preserving the original bug. We evaluate Rondo on four deep learning frameworks using 24 common model architectures. Rondo detects 117 bugs, including 35 stateful bugs. We submit 39 bug reports, including 18 for stateful bugs; developers confirm 35 reports, including 16 for stateful bugs, and fix 18 bugs, including 11 stateful bugs. Rondo achieves the highest behavior coverage and compiler Python source-line coverage among the compared methods, with 99.26% alarm precision. It shortens 44 of 117 invocation sequences, reducing the lengths of these 44 sequences by 83.34% on average.

papers.title: Developer Experiences with Cursor AI-native IDE
papers.abstract: AI-powered integrated development environments (IDEs) are increasingly positioned as practical tools for software development, integrating AI assistance into everyday activities such as editing, refactoring, and debugging. However, how developers evaluate AI IDEs as working environments, what frictions shape their adoption, and which aspects of the experience matter most in everyday use remain underexplored. Prior evidence on adoption and use is mainly controlled tasks, small interview samples, and short observation windows, which offer limited visibility into longitudinal, community-driven experience and the workflow drift that emerges in everyday practice. To bridge this gap, we conduct a large-scale longitudinal study of Cursor, a prominent AI-native IDE, through its official public forum, where users report bugs, request features, and discuss everyday use. Our analysis covers 14,714 forum posts collected over more than two years. We find that discussion is dominated by workflow-critical mechanisms (71%) such as context indexing, model routing, and agent workflows, which are also the main sources of both perceived value and frustration. Negative experiences center on usability, pricing, and dependability, including installation and setup, usage limits and consumption, crashes, and latency. Over time, the focus of friction shifts from early access and setup barriers toward pricing, robustness, and sustained workflow reliability.

papers.title: HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to optimize code, but existing benchmarks fix one accelerator, programming model or harness, so they cannot isolate what each component contributes or show whether added skills and tools repay their cost. We present HPCAgent-Bench with 689 kernels in three tracks: loop-level optimization challenges, kernels extracted from HPC codes, and machine-learning models. The framework specifies each kernel once in NumPy, derives C and Fortran references, accepts submissions through a common C ABI or Python interface, and runs them on CPUs or GPUs, on one or multiple nodes. An external judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and times each submission, closing paths agents use to exploit the testing system. We introduce two metrics for reporting results: \textit{intervention efficacy} measures an intervention, such as adding a tool, through paired runs on speedup, success rate and cost, and \textit{weighted token cost} reports input, cached-input and output tokens under explicit weights. Agents reach up to $4.2\times$ speedup over automatic parallelizers, and their optimizations transfer to another machine: $93$--$99\%$ of answers without device-specific code remain correct, and per-kernel speedups keep a rank correlation of $r_s\ge0.84$. Across 40 matched setups, interventions significantly change speedup only twice but token cost by up to $3.0\times$. Because token weighting decides whether a saving is significant, we state the weights and release every token count as a standard for cost reporting. We provide the first comprehensive, broad and hardened benchmark for the sound evaluation of agentic optimization, with transparent cost metrics.

papers.title: Robotic-supported Data Loss Detection in Android Applications
papers.abstract: Smartphones have become integral to modern life due to their diverse applications. However, the development of applications for these devices faces significant challenges, primarily due to two factors: (i) the diverse hardware and operating system versions that require testing across multiple configurations; and (ii) the imperative activity of testing the smartphone in a non-invasive way (similar to an end-user interaction), which is expensive, tedious and error-prone as it is usually carried out manually. In this context, robotic automation has emerged as an effective solution for addressing the diversity of smartphone systems and versions, and in performing some testing tasks non-invasively. In addition, automated robots facilitate quick, accurate, and repetitive testing, thus enabling developers to validate their applications across various configurations effectively. This results in a less invasive verification and in a significant reduction in time spent on manual testing, thus accelerating the development cycle. Our work proposes R-DLD (Robotic-supported Data Loss Detection), a robot-assisted infrastructure for data loss detection in Android applications, offeringless invasive and more realistic tests by interacting directly with smartphone sensors. The robot is constructed using cost-effective materials, facilitating its adoption in testing environments. In our empirical evaluation R-DLD successfully identified 341 data loss issues in 77 randomly selected apps from an Android store. All reported bugs received responses from the developer, with 89.55% confirming the data loss problems, while 35.82% have being subsequently fixed.

papers.title: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files
papers.abstract: A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold. Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits. Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark's tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.

papers.title: Plausible Is Not Enough: Trust and Evidence in AI-Authored Pull Request Review
papers.abstract: Code review is where AI-authored pull requests (AIPRs) must earn reviewer trust before integration, yet it is unclear whether reviewers apply the same criteria used for human-authored pull requests (HPRs). We surveyed 239 practitioners from 31 countries using matched HPR and AIPR questions to compare trust, evidence requirements, and verification practices within respondents. Most respondents (64.9%) reported lower initial trust in AIPRs. They relied less on author track record and subsystem familiarity, emphasizing instead human prompter expertise and bounded change size. For approval, respondents more often considered their own reasoning through critical cases sufficient for AIPRs than HPRs (55.2% versus 28.5%), while relying less on test coverage. Overall, 61.1% reported higher evidence requirements for AIPRs, and the share who would block approval under residual uncertainty increased from 19.4% for HPRs to 43.9% for AIPRs. Respondents prioritized test inspection, project context, and local execution, and more often selected partial reimplementation to verify non-trivial logic. Unclear ownership was also more likely to pause AIPR review (29.3% versus 14.6%). Open-ended responses pointed to the difficulty of validating plausible code without reliable context and human accountability. These findings frame AIPR review as an evidence-ownership problem, not merely a correctness check. Reviewers need to connect generated changes to validated behavior and responsible maintainers. Review tools and agentic workflows should expose provenance, distinguish generated claims from human-validated evidence, and make uncertainty visible before approval.

papers.title: Beyond Confidence: Rethinking Uncertainty Calibration in Deep Code Models
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have shown significant promise in code-related tasks. While confidence calibration techniques have been proposed to improve model reliability, their effectiveness in real-world tasks with strict accuracy requirements remains uncertain. In this paper, we investigate two key questions: first, whether existing measurement metrics, including confidence scores and uncertainty metrics, are effective for guiding selective prediction; and second, whether existing calibration techniques can improve these metrics to better identify cases where model predictions are likely to succeed or fail. We conduct a systematic study on defect prediction and vulnerability detection using seven code models, evaluating thirteen uncertainty signals and three widely used post-hoc calibration methods. Our analysis reveals three major findings: (1) even strong uncertainty signals can remain poorly calibrated and provide limited separation at the high-confidence end, constraining selective prediction in practice; (2) standard post-hoc calibrators often improve calibration scores but do not consistently translate into better selective prediction behavior; and (3) commonly used calibration metrics can disagree with selective prediction performance, underscoring the need to evaluate both jointly. Moreover, our findings motivate a decision-oriented view of reliability in deep code models, where calibrated scores must be evaluated together with selective-prediction quality and retained-region risk before they can support accept--defer deployment.

papers.title: When CONTRIBUTING Files Fall Short: Revising OSS Contribution Guidelines with Repository Evidence
papers.abstract: Contribution guidelines help newcomers participate in open-source software projects, yet often contain incomplete or outdated information. Existing studies characterize newcomers' information needs and documentation gaps, but revising these guidelines requires recovering and validating project-specific knowledge from scattered sources. We present ContribAlign, a framework for automatically revising CONTRIBUTING files through category-guided evidence integration. A qualitative analysis yields a taxonomy of 30 fine-grained guidance types across six contribution categories. ContribAlign uses a classifier to diagnose coverage of the six categories in the original guidance, then uses the taxonomy to collect and organize project-specific evidence. It filters detected conflicts and uses a large language model to generate category-level revisions. The classifier achieves a weighted F1 score of 0.764, improving on the existing classifier by 0.156, while the verifier detects factual conflicts with 97.3% precision and 91.5% estimated recall. Human evaluation shows that ContribAlign achieves the highest overall quality among the original guidelines and three baselines, with significant improvements in usefulness, beginner-friendliness, and completeness. These results suggest that ContribAlign can help maintain more accurate and useful contribution guidelines.

papers.title: SWE-at-Scale: Scalable Issue Synthesis from Historical Bug Fixes
papers.abstract: As coding agents become increasingly capable, robust evaluation requires a broader and more diverse supply of verifiable software engineering (SWE) tasks. However, real-world tasks are constrained by the natural frequency of issue reporting and the substantial cost of manual curation. Furthermore, existing synthetic approaches rely primarily on the pretrained knowledge of large models coupled with heuristic prompting, often failing to capture the authentic, complex mechanics of software failures. To exponentially scale SWE task production, we introduce SWE-at-Scale, a framework that automatically synthesizes realistic issues by reverse-engineering real-world software fixes. Our key insight is that historical fixes encapsulate deep mechanistic knowledge of bug formation: inverting a fix transforms repair supervision into bug-induction supervision grounded in actual development scenarios. SWE-at-Scale transfers these learned bug patterns to novel code contexts, repeatedly sampling diverse bug typologies to construct executable SWE tasks. Extensive experiments show that SWE-at-Scale generates more diverse and realistic SWE tasks than current synthesis baselines while posing greater challenges to state-of-the-art coding agents. Notably, SWE-at-Scale can generate distinct bug types from a single code context, with bug diversity scaling robustly even up to 200 generations per file. Overall, SWE-at-Scale turns finite real-world fixes into reusable supervision for scalable synthesis of realistic, diverse, and challenging SWE tasks.
